interview_transcripts.assessor_note: Answers covered the core requirements, but several examples stayed at a high level. Worth confirming isolation and migration experience in a follow-up.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Take a feature you owned end to end and walk me through it.

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: We added saved views to the reporting page. I wrote the migration, the query and the interface. It went out behind a flag and we removed the flag after a week.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you keep one customer's data out of another's view?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: The tenant id is on every table and the ORM adds the filter. I did not set that up, it was already there when I joined.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What happened the last time a migration went wrong?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: I have not had one fail in production. We run them off hours, so we would just restore if needed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you test that work?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Unit tests for the query layer. End-to-end is handled by our QA pair rather than by me.

interview_transcripts.assessor_note: Answers covered most requirements with concrete examples; database-level isolation and performance work stayed general.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Take a feature you owned end to end and walk me through it.

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Bulk invoicing. I designed the schema, wrote the migration in two additive steps so nothing blocked, then built the queue worker and the interface. Rollback was a single down migration we rehearsed on a copy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you keep one customer's data out of another's view?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Every query goes through a repository that requires a tenant id, and there is a test that fails if a query is built without one. We discussed row-level security but did not adopt it while I was there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The list view slows down at scale. What do you do?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Look at the slow query log first, then the plan. Usually it is a missing index or offset pagination, and I would move it to a cursor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you test that work?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Unit tests as standard, and I added the first end-to-end tests on that team for the invoicing path.

interview_transcripts.assessor_note: Answers tracked the requirements closely, with concrete examples and stated trade-offs for each.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Take a feature you owned end to end and walk me through it.

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Usage-based billing. Schema first, then a batched backfill of two years of events in chunks of fifty thousand with a resume point, then the API and the interface. The migration ran during the day because every step was additive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you keep one customer's data out of another's view?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Row-level security on every tenant table, with the policy taking the tenant from a session claim. The important part is the negative tests: for each table there is a test that sets a different tenant and asserts zero rows. Application filters alone drift the moment somebody writes raw SQL.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Where does that model bite you?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Admin and reporting paths. You need a deliberate, audited way to bypass it, and analytics queries get slower because the policy is applied per row.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you test the whole thing?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Unit for logic, integration against a real Postgres with the policies on, and one end-to-end path per feature. CI blocks the merge if any of the three go red.

interview_transcripts.assessor_note: Every requirement was answered with a worked example, a failure mode and a stated trade-off. No comprehension gaps in English.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Take a feature you owned end to end and walk me through it.

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: We split a shared table used by four teams into per-domain schemas with no maintenance window. Dual write, backfill in batches with a checksum comparison per batch, read switch behind a flag per tenant, then the old write path removed a fortnight later. Each step had its own rollback, and we practised the rollback before the step.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you keep one customer's data out of another's view?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Row-level security with the tenant taken from a verified claim, one policy per table and per operation. There is a generated test matrix that walks every table and role and asserts the deny case; it fails the build when someone adds a table without a policy.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is the cost of that decision?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Two things. Reporting needs an explicitly audited bypass, and plans change because the policy predicate joins into every query — we keep index coverage for the predicate itself. It is still cheaper than trusting application filters.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you keep the suite trustworthy?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Flaky tests are treated as broken tests: quarantined the same day with an owner, deleted if nobody fixes them in a week. A suite people ignore is worse than no suite.

interview_transcripts.assessor_note: Answered at architecture level throughout, with measurements, failure modes and the documentation trail behind each decision.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Take a feature you owned end to end and walk me through it.

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Partitioning the events table at four billion rows. I wrote the runbook, the rehearsal on a restored snapshot, and the abort criteria: if replication lag passed thirty seconds we stopped and rolled back. It shipped across three windows with no customer-visible downtime.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you approach tenant isolation at that size?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Row-level security as the floor, plus a generated policy audit in CI, plus a quarterly review that reads the policy set against the data map. The audit is what catches drift; a person reading policies once a year does not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you decide what to document?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Anything a new engineer would otherwise have to reconstruct from the code: the isolation model, the migration playbook, and the reasons behind the two decisions we would most like to revisit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you get wrong most often?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Underestimating how long a dual-write window needs to stay open. I now plan for twice the estimate and measure before removing the old path.
